slides.title: EBS persists within one Availability Zone
copy: EC2 uses a network block device in its own AZ.
A detached volume can attach to another compatible instance in the same AZ.
To move across AZs, create a new volume from a snapshot.
slides.layout: Two AZ islands; solid same-AZ attachment and a clearly separate snapshot bridge.

slides.title: EBS: choose the disk for the access pattern
copy: gp2/gp3 and io1/io2 are SSD boot or data volumes.
st1 handles frequent large sequential I/O; sc1 suits colder sequential data.
st1/sc1 are data only and cannot be boot volumes.
slides.layout: Three glossy workload lanes: SSD random I/O, provisioned SSD transactions, HDD sequential blocks.

slides.title: gp2 and gp3 separate capacity from performance differently
copy: gp2 baseline IOPS scales with volume capacity; smaller volumes can burst using credits.
gp3 lets you provision capacity, IOPS and throughput independently within supported limits.
io1/io2 serve provisioned-IOPS workloads; io2 emphasizes durability and consistent low latency.
slides.layout: Capacity, IOPS and throughput as independent tuning controls; gp2 capacity linkage contrasted with gp3.

slides.title: Find the narrowest point in the EBS path
copy: Application I/O size and concurrency affect useful throughput.
The volume has IOPS and throughput limits.
The instance also has EBS bandwidth and IOPS limits; increasing volume performance alone may not help.
slides.layout: A glossy data pipeline with three visible bottleneck valves: application, EC2, EBS.

slides.title: Snapshots capture changed blocks, not application intent
copy: After the first snapshot, later snapshots save changed blocks.
Quiesce applications and flush writes when application consistency is required.
Snapshots are managed by EBS; their backing S3 storage is not your ordinary bucket.
slides.layout: Three point-in-time block stacks highlighting only changed blocks plus an application flush gate.

slides.title: Restore in the target AZ and plan first-read latency
copy: Restore a snapshot into a new volume in the required AZ.
Restored blocks may initialize on first access; measure recovery performance.
Fast Snapshot Restore can provide fully initialized volumes in enabled AZs; it has additional cost.
slides.layout: Snapshot vault between AZs; new target volume with cold-to-ready blocks and optional FSR fast lane.

slides.title: Automate recovery points with the right policy service
copy: Data Lifecycle Manager manages policies for EBS snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs.
Tags identify resources; schedules and retention control lifecycle.
AWS Backup centralizes protection across supported services; test restore procedures.
slides.layout: A tagged EC2/EBS group under DLM and a wider multi-service AWS Backup vault, visually distinct scopes.

slides.title: Encryption needs a working recovery key
copy: EBS encryption by default is a per-Region account setting for new volumes and snapshot copies.
Enabling it does not encrypt existing unencrypted volumes in place.
Use snapshot-based migration and verify KMS permissions for copies, sharing and recovery.
slides.layout: Regional default-encryption switch, old unencrypted disk staying unchanged, snapshot-copy path to locked new disk.

slides.title: Multi-Attach shares a block device, not a normal file share
copy: Supported io1/io2 volumes can attach to multiple supported instances in the same AZ.
Every writer sees the same block device.
Use cluster-aware coordination and supported fencing; ordinary ext4/XFS shared mounting is unsafe.
slides.layout: One io2 block volume connected to two EC2 instances inside one AZ with a coordination lock between writers.

slides.title: Grow EBS deliberately; treat instance store as disposable
copy: Elastic Volumes can change supported volume size, type and performance; extend the OS filesystem too.
EBS cannot shrink in place: migrate data to a smaller new volume.
Instance store is host-local: reboot preserves it, but stop, termination or host loss can destroy it.
slides.layout: Persistent EBS growth control and OS resize step beside temporary host-local scratch bin.

slides.title: EFS shares files across clients and AZs
copy: EFS provides a managed NFS filesystem with POSIX semantics.
Regional storage spans AZs; One Zone accepts a single-AZ failure boundary.
Linux applications can share a file namespace without managing file servers.
slides.layout: Multiple Linux clients in two AZs mounting one regional shared file namespace, separate One Zone option.

slides.title: A mount target is the network doorway to EFS
copy: Mount targets expose network interfaces; clients need routes and NFS TCP 2049 access.
Prefer a mount target in the client AZ where available.
On-premises and peered clients need private connectivity, working DNS or target IPs, and return routing.
slides.layout: Local-AZ EFS mount doorway plus on-premises private network path; route and security-group gates.

slides.title: EFS authorization has several independent layers
copy: Security groups control network reachability; IAM policies can control ClientMount and ClientWrite.
POSIX ownership and permissions still control file access.
Access points enforce a root directory and POSIX identity; use TLS and KMS encryption.
slides.layout: Application entering network gate, IAM gate and POSIX directory gate via a dedicated access point.

slides.title: Choose EFS throughput to match demand
copy: General Purpose is recommended for current workloads; Max I/O is a previous-generation mode.
Elastic throughput scales with variable demand.
Provisioned throughput sets a chosen rate; Bursting depends on Standard storage and credits.
slides.layout: Variable workload stream matched to Elastic, steady reserved pipe for Provisioned, credit reservoir for Bursting.

slides.title: EFS lifecycle changes cost and access behavior
copy: Lifecycle policies move eligible files between Standard, Infrequent Access and Archive.
Colder classes trade lower storage cost for access charges and different latency.
Regional supports Archive; One Zone has a different storage-class set and failure boundary.
slides.layout: Frequently used files on bright warm shelf, idle files moving to IA and Archive tiers, Regional versus One Zone boundary.

slides.title: EFS replication is asynchronous recovery
copy: Replication maintains a destination filesystem in the same or another Region.
The protected destination is read-only while replication is active.
Plan failover, application remounts and recovery point monitoring; replication is not an independent backup history.
slides.layout: Primary regional file tree sending asynchronous updates to read-only destination, controlled failover gate.

slides.title: Choose FSx by filesystem semantics
copy: Windows File Server: SMB and Active Directory.
Lustre: parallel compute and S3-linked datasets.
ONTAP: NFS, SMB and iSCSI; OpenZFS: managed NFS with ZFS capabilities.
slides.layout: Four distinct filesystem workstations associated with their protocol and workload.

slides.title: Windows file shares keep Windows access controls
copy: FSx for Windows File Server provides managed SMB shares with NTFS semantics.
Active Directory, ACLs, quotas and DFS Namespaces support enterprise file workflows.
Compatible Linux SMB clients and on-premises clients can connect through supported private networking.
slides.layout: Windows user identity badge opening managed SMB share, NTFS ACL and quota labels, Linux SMB client and private on-prem path.

slides.title: Multi-AZ Windows file storage protects the server tier
copy: A Multi-AZ deployment uses active and standby file servers in different AZs.
Managed failover changes the serving node; clients must reconnect correctly.
Backups address recovery history; Multi-AZ alone does not undo accidental deletion.
slides.layout: Two AZs containing active and standby Windows file servers, distinct independent backup vault.

slides.title: Change Windows file-system layout through migration
copy: For Single-AZ to Multi-AZ, create a suitable target and migrate or restore a supported backup.
To reduce allocated storage, create a smaller target and copy data; do not assume in-place shrinking.
DataSync can support a staged copy, final synchronization, validation and application cutover.
slides.layout: Existing large Single-AZ share, staged DataSync bridge and smaller Multi-AZ target with deliberate cutover switch.

slides.title: Lustre feeds parallel compute
copy: FSx for Lustre supplies a shared parallel filesystem for HPC, ML and media workloads.
Many compute clients access a shared dataset concurrently.
Choose storage and throughput for the workload; S3 integration links an object repository to file processing.
slides.layout: HPC worker cluster consuming parallel bright data lanes from Lustre, S3 repository beside it.

slides.title: Lustre scratch and persistent protect different jobs
copy: Scratch suits temporary processing whose data can be recreated.
Persistent deployments replicate data within an AZ and replace failed servers.
Neither choice alone is cross-AZ disaster recovery; protect source data and important outputs separately.
slides.layout: Disposable scratch workspace contrasted with replicated same-AZ persistent workspace and separate durable source repository.

slides.title: Lazy loading brings the working set to Lustre
copy: A linked S3 repository can expose file metadata before every data block is loaded.
Reading an uncached file loads its content into Lustre.
Configure import and export behavior deliberately; changed outputs do not magically synchronize under every configuration.
slides.layout: S3 dataset with only selected working-set files lighting up across a lazy-load path into Lustre, explicit export arrow for results.

slides.title: ONTAP combines file and block protocols
copy: FSx for NetApp ONTAP serves NFS, SMB and iSCSI through storage virtual machines and volumes.
Snapshots, clones, compression and deduplication support enterprise data workflows.
SSD capacity and capacity-pool tiering are distinct; plan HA, networking and capacity rather than assuming unlimited auto-shrink.
slides.layout: ONTAP central system with NFS SMB iSCSI doors, snapshot clone branch, hot SSD and colder capacity pool tiers.

slides.title: OpenZFS brings ZFS capabilities to managed NFS
copy: FSx for OpenZFS provides NFS shares for compatible clients.
Snapshots and clones support testing and point-in-time workflows; compression reduces stored data where effective.
Select deployment, capacity and throughput explicitly; managed storage does not remove application recovery design.
slides.layout: NFS file tree on OpenZFS with space-efficient snapshot and clone branches, compression metaphor.

slides.title: S3 File Gateway translates file access into objects
copy: On-premises applications use NFS or SMB; the gateway caches active data locally.
File content is stored as S3 objects with asynchronous upload.
Plan cache capacity, upload health and external-change refresh; object access does not turn S3 into a general shared POSIX filesystem.
slides.layout: Office NFS/SMB clients, local cache appliance, buffered upload path to S3 object bucket.

slides.title: Volume Gateway: decide where the primary data lives
copy: Cached volumes keep primary data in AWS and a working set locally.
Stored volumes keep the full primary dataset locally and send snapshot backups to AWS.
Both expose iSCSI block volumes; local disks, connectivity and recovery requirements drive the choice.
slides.layout: Clearly contrasted cached and stored volume paths with primary-data badges and local cache versus full local data.

slides.title: Tape Gateway preserves the backup interface
copy: Existing backup software writes to an iSCSI virtual tape library.
Virtual tapes can move from online storage to archive for longer retention.
FSx File Gateway is a legacy option unavailable to new customers; use current supported designs for new deployments.
slides.layout: Backup application feeding virtual tape library then cloud archive, small separate legacy FSx gateway notice.

slides.title: EBS walkthrough: modify, extend and verify
copy: In a sandbox, inspect the volume AZ, attachment, encryption and performance settings.
Modify a supported volume; wait for the operation state, then extend the partition/filesystem as required.
Verify OS-visible capacity and workload performance; confirm snapshots and cleanup.
slides.layout: Clearly labelled illustrative console walkthrough, three original simplified educational panels Inspect, Modify and extend, Verify; not a real screenshot and no invented console status values.

slides.title: EFS walkthrough: mount, authorize and prove sharing
copy: Create a sandbox filesystem, mount target and narrow NFS security-group rule.
Mount with the EFS helper using TLS and required IAM/access-point options.
Write a test file from one authorized client, read it from another, then test a denied path and clean up.
slides.layout: Clearly labelled illustrative educational console walkthrough with network/security setup, two Linux client terminals and shared test file; no claim to be an actual AWS screenshot.

slides.title: A snapshot, an AMI and a regional recovery copy solve different jobs
copy: A snapshot preserves block data; an EBS-backed AMI references backing snapshots and supplies boot metadata.
Copy snapshots or AMIs to the recovery Region before a regional failure.
For encrypted copies, plan regional KMS keys, permissions and a tested instance launch.
slides.layout: Three recovery artifacts: data snapshot, launchable AMI with metadata, and separately prepared regional recovery copy; clear conceptual distinctions.

slides.title: DLM owns the recovery points created by its policies
copy: Tag target EC2 instances or EBS volumes; schedule snapshots or EBS-backed AMIs.
Retention and copy rules govern recovery points created by that DLM policy.
DLM does not take over arbitrary external snapshots or instance-store-backed AMIs; use AWS Backup for wider service governance.
slides.layout: Tagged resources pass through a DLM policy factory into owned snapshot and AMI lifecycle; external snapshots stay outside the factory.

slides.title: Choose file-storage performance without changing its semantics
copy: FSx for Windows offers SSD and HDD storage; latency-sensitive and metadata-heavy work usually needs SSD.
Lustre storage and throughput choices must fit parallel small-random or large-sequential I/O.
ONTAP and OpenZFS add snapshots, clones and space efficiency; clients still need the correct protocol, networking and capacity plan.
slides.layout: Windows metadata search on SSD versus sequential shared files on HDD; parallel Lustre lane; snapshot clone tree for ONTAP/OpenZFS.

slides.title: Deploy a gateway with identity, cache and recovery in mind
copy: S3 File Gateway uses a bucket-access IAM role; SMB can authenticate with Active Directory.
Plan local cache and upload capacity; archive lifecycle rules can require object restore before file access.
Choose a supported virtual deployment for new systems. FSx File Gateway is closed to new customers; the AWS hardware appliance is no longer sold.
slides.layout: Gateway with IAM bucket-key and AD user badges, local cache/upload buffer, S3 lifecycle to archive with restore gate; separate small legacy hardware and FSx gateway notice.
